lead.headline: Not every outage is an AI attack
lead.summary: Three distinct signals point to a practical question: who can safely intervene when a system fails?

stories.title: The FAA reported no indication of a cyberattack
stories.summary: The FAA says instability affected 17 of 22 en-route control centres before its 13 November nationwide ground stop. The agency reported that some radio and radar functions remained available and flights already airborne landed safely. In its 15 November account, it reported no indication of cyberattack and said the root cause was still under investigation. That day’s cancellation total is not a count of flights cancelled because of the ground stop. The case demonstrates a decision to pause on safety grounds, not proof the fallback worked equally well for everyone.

stories.title: One investigation does not establish prevalence
stories.summary: On 20 November, Amazon Threat Intelligence reported observing autonomous AI agents used in a September intrusion campaign. This is a first-party account of a specific investigation, not a global incident count or independent proof of actor identity. The operational lesson is to limit tool and data access, monitor actions outside scope and rehearse how an authorised person stops a run.

stories.title: A compromised AI dependency is not evidence of AI authorship
stories.summary: GitHub’s malware advisory identifies two malicious agent-framework releases, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, which it says were removed from PyPI. The advisory does not establish how many installations were affected or whether an AI system authored the malware. If exposure is suspected, use the organisation’s incident-response process to isolate and rebuild affected environments, review accessible credentials and rotate them as appropriate.

stories.title: A software update is not proof of a safe outcome
stories.summary: The 6 November NHTSA recall query examines the adequacy of an earlier Waymo school-bus remedy and post-remedy reports. This is a continuing watchpoint, not a new filing this week or a final finding. It does not establish a population-wide incident rate or that a subsequent remedy works. Request evidence for the deployed configuration in representative conditions, including the experience of people who did not choose to be near an automated vehicle.

stories.title: Design and rehearse the human fallback
stories.summary: Australian cyber guidance recommends containing AI agents during testing, monitoring activity and keeping human oversight rather than relying only on prompts. For a critical workflow, identify the person who can pause the system, the usable fallback and the route for people to correct an error. Record what happened during a representative, authorised test and repeat it after material changes. This is a DΩP recommendation, not a claim of industry adoption or certification.

outlook.label: Practise the fallback before launch
outlook.summary: Name the person who can intervene. Test a usable fallback in representative conditions and record what worked, what failed and who can correct the result.

report.title: Not every outage is an AI attack
report.standfirst: What infrastructure outages, agent misuse and compromised software teach us about keeping people in control.
report.intro: This edition separates a documented service disruption, a first-party account of agent misuse and a malware advisory. They are not evidence of a shared cause. We keep the robotics inquiry as a continuing watchpoint, and do not assign a global risk or human agency score.

investigativeSummary: The regulator’s 15 November account separates the 13 November nationwide precautionary stop from any confirmed malicious act. It reports instability at 17 of 22 en-route centres, some still-operational radio and radar functions, and safe landings. The FAA said there was no indication of cyberattack and the precise root cause was still under investigation. Record availability, confirmed cause and the effect of safeguards as separate questions.
